title: Why Is the Sky Blue but Sunsets Red? #sky #physics
description:
Same sun, same air: only the path through the air changes. Air molecules scatter blue light about 6 times more strongly than red, so blue reaches you from every direction. At sunset the light crosses about 38 times more air: less than a thousandth of the blue survives, about a quarter of the red does.

Full episode: Why is the sky blue but sunsets red? https://youtu.be/H_61WImrwoQ

Sources
- Bodhaine et al. (1999), On Rayleigh optical depth calculations, J. Atmos. Oceanic Technol. 16: 1854–1861
- Kasten & Young (1989), Revised optical air mass tables and approximation formula, Applied Optics 28: 4735–4738
- NOAA NESDIS, Why is the sky blue?
- NASA Space Place, Why is the sky blue?

Next sunset you watch, remember: someone to the west is getting your blue.

subtitles: Why is the sky blue, but the sunset red?
Only the path through the air changes.
Sunlight is every colour mixed together.
Air molecules knock some of it sideways, and they scatter blue about six times more strongly than red.
That scattered blue reaches you from every direction.
At sunset, the light skims in almost flat, through about 38 times more air.
Even in clean air, less than a thousandth of the blue survives that trip.
About a quarter of the red does.
So the sun glows orange and red.
Somebody to the west gets it, as their afternoon sky.
